claims.text: The degree of local chemical short-range order governs strength and deformation behavior in multi-component concentrated alloys.
Chemical short-range order locally alters bond strength.
Chemical short-range order alters local lattice friction.
Greater chemical short-range order increases yield strength.
Chemical short-range order modifies strain-hardening behavior.
Rapid quenching from the homogenization temperature produces a nearly random solid-solution microstructure with minimal short-range order.
Controlled annealing can increase short-range order relative to rapid quenching.
The thermal treatments can vary short-range order without significantly changing overall composition or grain size.
Preferred local atomic arrangements modify dislocation core structure.
Increased short-range order raises local energy barriers for dislocation motion by changing the chemical environment at slip planes.
The higher barriers to dislocation motion lead to higher yield strength.
Excessive inhibition of dislocation activity by short-range order could promote more brittle failure.
An annealed state with enhanced short-range order will have a different work-hardening profile than a rapidly quenched baseline.
Changes in local bonding and atomic spacing caused by short-range order will alter dislocation dynamics.
Changes in short-range order may change the failure mode.
The proposed relationship applies when solid-solution strengthening dominates over precipitation and grain-boundary strengthening.
The proposed relationship applies within a temperature window where diffusion permits short-range ordering without secondary-phase formation.
Diffuse-scattering measurements or atom-probe tomography can be used to quantify the degree of short-range order in the compared samples.
